1:
The first word divides them four ways. Gill takes it as empty of fruit, not of temporal good things but of spiritual fruit, being destitute of the Spirit; he allows an alternative, an emptying vine that casts its fruit before it is ripe, and applies it to a people who emptied themselves of wealth by sending presents to foreign princes or consuming it on their idols. Wesley takes the plain sense, a vine that has lost its strength to bring forth fruit. Clarke gives the alternative as his own rendering, a vine that casteth its grapes. Calvin says those who make the word mean empty are mistaken, since the verb properly means to pillage or to plunder: Israel is like a vine robbed after the ingathering has come, and this view he thinks best suits the place. Ellicott rejects the received rendering outright as inconsistent with what follows, and reads luxuriant instead, appealing to the Greek and Latin versions.

Ellicott builds a history on that reading. The metaphors of the vintage are still in the mind of the prophet, and one scholar has powerfully illustrated the wild strong growth of the northern kingdom compared with the southern: one of its kings plundered the capital of the south, another extended his power as far as Hamath, and the kingdom had resisted the attacks of Syria and become insolent as well as idolatrous. He renders the last clause to bring out the proportion, that the more abundant his fruit the more he increased altars, and the fairer his land the fairer the pillars; and he explains the logic of it: misapprehending the cause of their prosperity and wilfully ignoring the forbearance of God, they attributed their mercies to the grace of an idol and multiplied its shrines.

Clarke reads the same proportion morally. Israel was prosperous, but prosperity corrupted the heart, so that he became idolatrous in proportion to his prosperity, and in proportion to their wealth was the costliness of their images and the expensiveness of their idol worship. He supports it with two poets and an apostle: an old English rhyme that the best gifts of God, usurped by wicked ones, turn to poison by their contagion; a line of Ovid that riches are dug up as the incitements to evil; and the saying that the love of money is the root of all these evils. Wesley makes the same connection in a line: the plenty of the land was employed on multiplying idols, and they imagined the goodness of their land a blessing from those idols.

Henry takes the emptiness as the root of all the rest. All their other wickedness began here, he says, since the church is fitly compared to a vine, weak and of an unpromising outside yet spreading and fruitful, whereas this vine had no sap or virtue in it and so produced none of the fruit by which God and man should be honoured. He draws the note out: many who have not become degenerate vines are yet empty vines with no good in them; a vine is of all trees least serviceable if it bear no fruit, and is thenceforth good for nothing; and those that bring forth no grapes will soon bring forth wild ones, since those who do no good will do hurt. On the second clause Henry sets self against God: what good there is in such a man is not directed to the glory of God, but he takes the praise to himself, since Christians live not to themselves while hypocrites make self their centre. Calvin, for his part, reports and sets aside two further renderings, one making the fruit lie to him, so that the vineyard yields nothing after robbers have passed, and one reading the clause as a question, whether Israel will lay up fruit for himself, which would mean the plundering was past all restitution.
2:
The divided heart is read in several directions. Gill lists them: divided from one another by discords and civil wars, and by disagreement about which idol to prefer; or from God himself and his worship; or, with the Targum, from the law; or divided between God and an idol, since they pretended to worship God when they worshipped the calves. He offers a further rendering, that their heart flatters them, as if they had done what was right and no punishment would follow. Clarke states it as the impossible attempt to serve two masters. Ellicott notes that the received rendering has the ancient versions and two Jewish commentators behind it, but that modern expositors prefer to translate that their heart is treacherous, or smooth; he corrects the clauses following to read that God will break the horns of their altars and destroy their pillars.

Calvin makes the division a breach of marriage. God binds us to himself by a holy union, so that it is the summit of all wickedness when the heart is divided from him, as when an unchaste wife alienates her affection from her husband: while he keeps her heart tied to himself, conjugal fidelity continues, but when it is divided it is all over. On the next clause he takes the verb to refer not to the deed but to its manifestation, so that to be found faulty means to be convicted, as to be justified means to be absolved.

The confession that they have no king is dated in different ways. Gill offers four: that they said it while they had one, having no regard for him; or during the interval between the murder of one king and the settling of another; or when the land was invaded and the king shut up; or, as he prefers, when the city was taken and they and their king carried captive. Clarke reads it as a confession of the real loss, that they had rejected the King of kings, any king they had being of no service in that state, a captive like themselves. Ellicott says the prophet, having witnessed a succession of kings overthrown and the anarchy that followed, predicts yet another time of confusion, a full vindication of the old warning about kings. Wesley says it in six words, that kings cannot save without the God of kings. Calvin hears the words as a confession wrung out of them: as long as God spared them they abused his forbearance and contended petulantly with the prophets, so that they would be taken into another school, where he would strike with his hand rather than remonstrate in words.

The false swearing is referred to different covenants. Gill takes in everything: idle words in conversation, deceit in trade, vain oaths, and covenants broken with God, with their own king, and with foreign princes. Clarke restricts it to alliances made with foreign powers, promised with no intention of fidelity; Wesley names the northern power. Calvin distinguishes two readings of the first clause, one making it that they daringly followed their own counsels without inquiring what is right, and one, which he prefers, making it that they very freely testified they would be the most faithful worshippers of God; on the covenant he holds the perjury was toward God, a mere dissimulation. Ellicott says the judgments will prevail not as a blessing but as a curse, not as a precious harvest but as a poisonous plant in the ridges of the field. Clarke draws it out: as the land lies uncultivated and yields noxious weeds instead of crops, so there is no administration of justice, and what is done in its name is as hurtful to society as hemlock to animal life. Keil and Delitzsch say the dissimulation of heart showed itself in their speaking words which were nothing but words.
5:
The feminine plural is heard as contempt by three. Gill renders it cow calves, so called by way of derision to denote their inability to help their worshippers, and notes that the place of one of them is here named the house of iniquity by way of contempt. Ellicott says it is hard to express the sarcastic force and concentrated scoff of the original, the feminine form expressing contempt and the plural alluding to the scattered worship in numerous shrines. Calvin says the prophet might have used the masculine and calls them heifers by way of contempt, the verse glancing at the madness of a people so grossly delirious in their superstitions and yet wholly insensible.

The verb is disputed. Calvin reports interpreters who expound the verse of the exile of the people, since the word can mean to be banished as well as to fear, but says the context will not allow it. Clarke reports another reading, following Calmet, that they shall worship the calves, fear being often taken for religious reverence. On the priests, Clarke says the word means black coats or shouters, so called because they made loud cries in their sacrifices; Ellicott says the term always means an idolatrous priesthood. Clarke also proposes reading howled for rejoiced, which he says the necessity of the place requires, though no manuscript yet discovered supports it.

The carrying away of the calf is the sting of the passage. Gill takes the pronoun of the calf itself rather than the people, and offers two accounts of who sent it: the people, to appease the foreign king, or rather the invading army, which reserved the plunder as a present for their conqueror, to whom not only nations but the gods of nations were subject. Ellicott renders it that the calf shall be carried in triumphant state as an offering. Calvin thinks the king was constrained by extreme danger to break up the image in order to redeem peace, and hears an emphasis in the connecting particle: not only shall the people migrate, but the very calf shall be carried away. He turns the whole into a ridicule of the worshippers, constrained to weep for the exile of their calf, so far is it from bringing them aid; and he asks why the gods do not help themselves instead of expecting help from mortals. On the name of the king, Clarke says that if it is a proper name the person is not known in history, and thinks another king intended. Calvin reports the guesses, that it was the name of a man, or a city not noticed by writers, or a neighbouring king, and holds that the passage refutes the last, since the prophet clearly points at the one power.

The figure for the king is the last thing they weigh. Clarke reads it as a puff of wind blowing off the foam formed below a fall of water, and recalls that four kings died by assassination in a very short time. Wesley says the prophecy was probably delivered when the city was besieged. Ellicott calls it one of the most striking images in the prophecy and corrects the rendering: the word properly signifies a chip or fragment, so that the king is tossed on the raging seas of political life like a helpless fragment. Keil and Delitzsch render it a splinter on the surface of the water, and take the name of the city absolutely, as for Samaria. Calvin keeps the foam and gets two things from it: the kingdom they imagined firm and perpetual had nothing in it but an empty appearance; and the foam that floats above the sea and seems eminent by its height is nothing but the excrement of the water, so that a kingdom which thought to ride over the head of its neighbour was in fact only that.
8:
The name of the place carries the argument. Gill notes that it is here called not merely the house of iniquity, as before, but iniquity itself, and takes the high places for the temple and altars built there, which were usually set on hills and mountains. Wesley names them the temples and altars of the idol. Calvin explains why the name was changed. The founder of that worship might have disguised what he profanely introduced by pleading that God had appeared in the place to the patriarch, and that its name had been given by God himself; but since the people made a wrong use of that example, the place was called the house of iniquity, as though the prophet said that God does not dwell there as superstitious men imagine, since it has been corrupted by ungodly worshippers. Calvin draws the general rule, that when men degenerate from the pure teaching of God they in vain cover their profanations with empty names.

Calvin also explains why the threatening is so prolonged. Much is dwelt on one thing, he grants, but there was need of a strong hammer to beat this iron, since the hearts of the people were iron or even steel, and such hardness could not be broken except with violence; a brief reminder would have sufficed had they not been so perverse, which is why the vengeance of God is placed before their eyes in so many forms.

The thorn and thistle are read as desolation and as curse. Clarke takes them for the uncultivated and unfrequented state of the land and of the places of idol worship, the people being all carried away into captivity. Ellicott identifies them as part of the first curse pronounced upon Adam, and says the prophet predicts not only utter ruin for king and calf, temple and shrine, but the future desolation which should conceal all of it.

The cry to the mountains is traced through the later Scriptures. Clarke quotes a note observing that this sublime description of fear and distress was had in view by our Lord, which may be a reference rather than a quotation, though the Greek in one great manuscript has the same order of words as the evangelist; the parallelism, it adds, makes the passage more beautiful than a place in the Revelation, while another prophet wants the animated dramatic form. Clarke adds a reference to the caverns which abounded in the mountainous parts of the country. Ellicott makes the same connections more briefly, naming the use of the words concerning the terrors of the impenitent in the fall of Jerusalem and twice in the Revelation, to denote the extremity of despair, and adding that meanwhile the people shall desire death rather than life. Wesley says only that the idolaters shall be in such perplexity that they will wish the mountains and hills might fall on them. Keil and Delitzsch mark the structure at this point, noting that after the threatening has been extended to the utter ruin of the kingdom the prophet returns to earlier times, in order to exhibit the deeply rooted sinfulness of the people in a new form, and then, under cover of an appeal to return to righteousness, to depict the time of visitation and predict with still greater clearness the overthrow of the monarchy.
9:
The reference is agreed: the outrage of the Levite and his concubine and the war that followed, not, as some suppose, the choosing of the first king who came from that place. Gill says so expressly against the Targum and others, and Clarke names the same episode. Gill offers two constructions: that the sins were not new but the same as those committed then and continued ever since, the measure now filling up; or, with two Jewish commentators, that they had sinned more than in the days of Gibeah, being guilty of greater idolatry and inhumanity and impurity than in those times, though the grossest of sins were then committed. Henry gives both readings likewise, and adds that not only was the wickedness of that age revived and reacted as a copy from the original, but it had been continued in a constant series and succession through all the intervening ages, so that the measure had been long in filling.

Calvin makes the point the length of the habit. He had said in the previous chapter that they were deep in their sins as in the days of Gibeah, because the men of that place had fallen away from all fear of God as though not a word of the law had ever been heard among them, abandoning themselves to lusts like the men of Sodom; but here he regards another thing, that from that time they had not ceased to accumulate evils on evils and to spin a continuous rope of iniquity. He raises the obvious objection against himself: the whole people united against the offending tribe and revenged the wickedness, so why is the crime charged on the avengers? His answer is that it often happens that those who execute the vengeance of God are in no respect better, and he cites the king who was the minister of God in punishing superstitions and is nevertheless called a robber, the vengeance he executed being compared to robbery.

The middle clause is read three ways. Gill and Henry take the standing as the criminals standing in their own defence, Henry adding that the tribes who undertook to chastise them were at a stand, since in the first and second battles the malefactors were the victors, and the war did not overtake them until the third engagement, and then not all of them, since six hundred escaped. Clarke says only one tribe was nearly destroyed, its men being the children of iniquity while the rest were faultless and stood only for the rights of justice and mercy. Wesley identifies the men who escaped as the six hundred who fled to the rock, and says the fatal battle did not reach them, whereas now the punishment shall be severer. Ellicott renders the clause differently, as remaining and sinning after the same manner.

The last clause divides Ellicott from others. He would render it as a question, whether the war made against the wicked shall not overtake them in Gibeah, the place being used mystically; he reports that Pusey and others take it categorically instead, so that though the exterminating war did not overtake them then and has not yet, it shall now and soon; but he prefers the former. He also fixes the date of the charge, that the transgressions began long before the division of the kingdom, and explains why the place is named, since it is emblematic of gross and cruel sensuality just as another city is used for unnatural vice. Henry, having set the sin, states the consequence in the same breath: the sin of this generation is worse than that of the former, and therefore they cannot expect but that the battle against the children of iniquity should overtake them and overcome them.
10:
The desire to chastise is the first difficulty. Gill renders it either that God will chastise or that he will bind them and carry them captive, and says he had this in his heart and would do it with pleasure for the glorifying of his justice. Calvin faces the objection that this seems repugnant to many other places where God declares his sorrow at being constrained to deal severely, and answers that the two are not discordant: passions do not belong to God, but in condescension to human capacity he puts on this or that character, so that when he seems unwilling to punish he shows with what tender affection he loves his own, and when he has to do with irreclaimable men he says he will take pleasure in their destruction.

The two furrows are variously identified. Clarke reports a rendering that makes it a chastisement for their two iniquities, meaning the two calves, and adds another from a prophet who charged the people with two evils, forsaking God and joining themselves to idols. Ellicott renders it the same way, taking the two iniquities for the calves which had been the source of heresy and treason. Wesley names the gathered people as the invaders, and guesses the two transgressions to be the revolt from the house of David and idolatry. Calvin passes over the number and dwells on the gathering: God shows that all peoples are in his hand and that he can arm them whenever he pleases, holding them so under his command that by a hiss or a nod he can stir them up to war.

The trained heifer turns on the difference between two kinds of work. Gill explains the husbandry: oxen were used both in ploughing and in treading out corn, and the heifer prefers the treading, where its mouth was not muzzled and it could feed. He applies it to a people taught to bear the yoke of the law who did not like such a course of life, and who by doing little and living well grew fat and proud and rent themselves from the house of David. Clarke gives the operations in order, treading out the corn that there may be seed, ploughing that the furrows may receive it, and harrowing that the seed may be covered. Wesley makes the reversal the point: the less sinful people had ploughed while the other reaped, but though they sow in tears going into exile they shall reap in joy at their return.

Calvin and the rest weigh the same contrast differently. Calvin reports interpreters who separate the first two words so as to make the opening a reproach, that Ephraim was wholly unteachable; he calls that too far fetched and follows the more approved reading, that Ephraim was accustomed to love threshing. The implied comparison is between ploughing and threshing: there is more labour in the first, where the oxen are coupled and compelled to obey, whereas in threshing they are loose. So Ephraim pretended some obedience without taking the yoke; other nations did not know what it was to obey God, but here there was an appearance of religion, which the Lord derides as the hypocrisy of a beast that passes through the threshing-floor for recreation. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion from the law: the animal loved threshing not because it was easier but because there the ox was allowed to eat at pleasure, from which the people grew fat and strong. Ellicott allows a second possibility, that the treading may point to the rough treatment this people dealt its neighbours, but thinks the first more probable; he renders the last clauses that God passed by the fairness of her neck to arrest her self-indulgence, and will harness her for riding, causing a rider to take possession of her so that she is bound in unwelcome toil.
12:
The call to sow in righteousness is heard by most as a genuine offer. Gill sets aside two senses of the seed, the seed of grace, which bad men cannot sow and good men need not, and the seed of the word, and prefers works of righteousness, since as sowing to the flesh is doing the works of the flesh, so sowing to righteousness is living soberly and righteously; and he notes that it is sowing to themselves, since such works, though they merit nothing at the hand of God, turn to the account of those that do them. Clarke turns it into husbandry: let the seed be of the best kind and in just measure, and by the blessing of God on this ploughing and sowing a good crop may be expected. He presses the urgency: this should be done immediately, since the season is passing, and if the seed is not got into the ground the early rain will be past and the fields unfruitful. He lists the operations the passage contains and says all may be applied to the human heart.

Ellicott hears it as a break in the weather. In their despair, he says, come characteristic gleams of hope on the desolation, since the eternal law which makes reaping a consequence of sowing still applies, and the mercy of God will be the harvest of a sowing to the Spirit; the soil of the soul is fallow and unbroken, and if they break it up and seek God he will come as never before. This momentary rift in the storm-cloud shows the light behind it. Wesley reads the fallow ground the same way, as hearts overrun with weeds which need to be broken up that good seed may be sown in them. Keil and Delitzsch supply the grammar: the sowing is that righteousness may spring up like seed, and its fruit will be a condescending love toward the poor and wretched; the phrase about the fallow means to plough virgin soil, which they call an advance in the figure.

Calvin alone denies that it is a simple exhortation. It seems to him rather a protestation, as though God said that he had hitherto laboured in vain, because the people had ever continued obstinate; and the next verse is his reason, since it relates how much God had done to restore them, so that the charge is one of obduracy in not growing better though often admonished. Yet Calvin holds the offer real: God tried whether they were healable, the remedy being that they should know he would be pacified toward them if they devoted themselves to righteousness. He answers the question whether it is in the power of men to sow righteousness by saying that the prophet does not explain how far human ability extends but requires what men ought to do.

The counter-charge is agreed. Gill takes the ploughing of wickedness as contriving it with much pains, and reads it of the first sins from which all others arose, irreligion and apostasy and idolatry and contempt of the prophets. Clarke glosses each clause: they laboured sinfully, reaped the punishment due to iniquity, and ate the fruit of lies, their false worship having brought them into captivity. Wesley identifies the two lies they lived on: their idolatry, which was their way, and the valour of their great men. Calvin says the people heard the call daily and had their ears almost stunned by it, and yet as with a fixed purpose ploughed ungodliness and reaped iniquity, so that they ate the fruit of falsehood, either sustaining just punishments or satiating themselves with treachery. Ellicott notes a variant on the word for their way: a slight change gives thy chariots, a reading followed by the Greek and by several moderns, which establishes a good parallelism, though he grants that the received text gives a fine meaning.
14:
The tumult is the invasion. Gill has the army entering and causing a noise of crying and howling through all the cities, especially among the fearful, and quotes Jarchi for a voice of clamour crying flee. Clarke says the enemy shall fall upon the people and take all their fortified places. Calvin puts the point of the word: the progress would not be slow, but the tumult would arise in one moment on every side and confound things from one corner of the land to the other, and whatever strength the people had would prove weak and useless. He notes that the noun can mean perdition or destruction but prefers tumult, the verb seeming to require it. Ellicott hears it as the crash of the thunder-peal, the prophet seeming to hear the advance of the invading army and to see the fall of the fortress of the capital.

The historical allusion in the next clause defeats everyone. Clarke reports two guesses, one referring it to the victory of a judge over a Midianite general, the other to the destruction of a city in Armenia by the conqueror named here, while he was still only a general and not yet king; but Clarke thinks the history unknown, and says that when and where and how and by whom the atrocity was done still remain unknown, so that conjecture in such a case must be useless. Ellicott says the allusion is very obscure and reports three theories from two scholars: an episode in a campaign to the cedar country or to Damascus, from which the king might have penetrated beyond the Jordan and destroyed the town named; a mention of a Moabitish king whose name occurs in an inscription, which Ellicott calls far-fetched and improbable; and, following a hint of Jerome, the identification of the name with the Midianite general. He notes that the kind of barbarity referred to is illustrated elsewhere in the Scriptures. Calvin says only that the town lay beyond the Jordan, and thinks the prophet was reviving the memory of a recent slaughter, though he notes that the name given here is a simple form and it is not known whether the prophet wrote it so. Wesley places the town in the northern empire and says it gave name to a region there.

The last verse turns the blame back on the shrine. Gill takes the phrase about the evil of their evil as extreme wickedness, and names it: the worshipping of the calf, which was the procuring cause of all their ruin, God being the cause and the foreign king the instrument. He offers a second rendering, that the same shall be done to the shrine itself as was done to the town beyond the Jordan. Calvin makes the same point the reason for the strange construction: the prophet might have said that God would do this to them, but says instead that the shrine would, so as to show more distinctly that the cause of the evil was in themselves, since the war did not arise from that place, and yet the slaughter is to be imputed to the corruption which had arisen there rather than to the invader. Wesley says it in a line, that the idolatry committed there procured all this evil. On the last clause Clarke reads the morning as suddenness and unexpectedness; Wesley suggests the assault may have been made towards morning; and Ellicott renders it in the early morning and says the last king was utterly cut off, leaving neither root nor branch. Clarke closes by admitting that there are allusions in this chapter which cannot easily be verified, for want of sufficient acquaintance with the history of those times.
